issues.legal_issue: Whether an appellate decree is one of affirmance when it changes the trial court’s decision on the merits, including by a change in favour of the party seeking a further appeal.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed a suit for a share of family properties after upholding the challenged alienations.
The appellate court held some alienations not binding on the plaintiff’s share and granted partition relief for the affected properties, while confirming the trial court’s decree as to the rest.
The plaintiff sought a certificate to appeal further, and the High Court refused it on the ground that its decree was one of affirmance.
issues.conclusion: An appellate decree must be compared as a whole with the trial court’s decision as a whole. A merits variation makes it a decree of variation, whether the variation is minor or major and whether it favours or disfavors the party seeking the further appeal. The refusal of the certificate was set aside and the matter remitted to the High Court for disposal according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 133(1) of the Constitution, the words concerning a decree that affirms the decision below refer to the appellate decree and trial court decision taken as wholes; “appealed from” is descriptive, not a limitation to the portion challenged in a further appeal. The natural meaning of “decision” is the decision of the suit as a whole, consistent with Rajah Tasadduq Rasul Khan v. Manik Chand. The Court disapproved the approach in Chittam Subba Rao v. Vela Mankanni Chellamayya and discussed Annapurnabai v. Ruprao as supporting the conclusion that a variation in favour of the intending appellant prevents the decree from being one of affirmance.

rule.if: constitutional_civil_appeal and appellate_court_adjudicated_a_merits_variation and not variation_is_only_costs and not variation_is_by_concession_consent_or_withdrawal

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_adjudicated_a_merits_var: The appellate court changed the trial court’s decision through its adjudication of the merits.
predicates.variation_is_only_costs: The only change made by the appellate court concerns costs.
predicates.variation_is_by_concession_consent_or_wi: The change resulted from a concession, the parties’ consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter rather than the appellate court’s decision on the merits.

issues.definition: When a civil appellate court adjudicates a merits change, and the change is neither only about costs nor caused by concession, consent, or withdrawal, the appellate decree is not one of affirmance.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a change confined to costs changes an appellate decree that otherwise affirms the trial court’s decision.
material_facts: The Court considered how a change to the costs order affects the character of an appellate decree that otherwise confirms the trial court’s decision.
Costs are within the court’s discretion under the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: A change confined to costs does not change the character of an appellate decree that is otherwise one of affirmance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court discretion over costs; a costs-only variation is not a variation of the decision on the merits for purposes of the affirmance test under Article 133(1) of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.appellate_decree_otherwise_affirms_trial: Apart from the costs order, the appellate decree confirms the trial court’s decision.
predicates.variation_is_only_costs: The only change made by the appellate court concerns costs.

issues.definition: If an appellate decree otherwise confirms the trial court’s decision and changes only costs, it remains one of affirmance.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a change to an award of interest affects the character of an appellate decree as one of affirmance.
material_facts: The Court distinguished interest from costs, explaining that interest forms part of the dispute between the parties.
The appellate court can award interest under the Code of Civil Procedure, and a change to that award can vary the decision.
issues.conclusion: A change to the award of interest affects the character of the appellate decree and makes it a decree of variation rather than affirmance.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, interest forms part of the dispute between the parties; a change to the interest award is therefore an integral variation of the decision for purposes of Article 133(1) of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_changed_interest_awarded: The appellate court changed the interest award that formed part of the dispute between the parties.

issues.definition: When an appellate court changes interest awarded as part of the dispute in a civil appeal, its decree is not one of affirmance.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a change resulting from concession, consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter changes the character of an appellate decree.
material_facts: The Court considered changes made because a party conceded a point, the parties consented to a change, or part of the subject matter covered by the decree was withdrawn.
Such a change does not result from the appellate court’s adjudication of the appeal on the merits.
issues.conclusion: A change resulting from concession, consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter does not affect the character of the appellate decree.
issues.legal_principle: The affirmance test under Article 133(1) of the Constitution concerns the appellate court’s decision on the merits; a change made by concession or consent, or following withdrawal of part of the subject matter, is not a merits variation by the appellate court.

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.change_results_from_concession_consent_o: The change resulted from a concession, the parties’ consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a change resulting from concession, consent, or withdrawal does not alter the appellate decree’s character.

issues.legal_issue: Whether the valuation condition for a further appeal controls the separate test for deciding if an appellate decree affirms the trial court’s decision.
material_facts: The case satisfied the valuation test under Article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution.
The Court considered whether that valuation condition affected the meaning of the separate affirmance requirement in Article 133(1).
issues.conclusion: The valuation test is an independent additional condition and does not control the meaning or application of the affirmance test.
issues.legal_principle: Article 133(1)(a) sets an independent condition concerning the value of the subject matter in dispute; it cannot control the construction of the separate provision concerning a decree that affirms the decision below. The Court also considered Raja Sree Nath Roy Bahadur v. The Secretary of State for India in Council, Annapurnabai v. Ruprao, and Narendra Lal Das Chaudhury v. Gopendya Lal Das Chaudhury in reviewing the earlier approaches to the affirmance test.

predicates.civil_appeal_under_constitutional_certif: The proceeding is a civil appeal for which a constitutional certificate provision sets conditions for a further appeal.
predicates.valuation_is_a_separate_eligibility_cond: The value of the subject matter is assessed as a distinct condition for further-appeal eligibility.

issues.definition: When value is a distinct eligibility condition in a civil appeal, it does not determine how the affirmance test applies.
